client: I've been really anxious about this weekend because I'm supposed to meet my partner's friends for the first time, and I just can't stop thinking that they're not going to like me. It's been keeping me up at night, going over all the ways it could go wrong. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to make the anxiety go away, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when you're not sure it'll help, and I'm glad you did. It sounds like your mind has been working overtime, running through worst-case scenarios and robbing you of sleep — that kind of anticipatory anxiety can feel exhausting and very real. I'd love to gently explore those thoughts with you: when you imagine them not liking you, what's the specific story your mind is telling you about what that would *mean*?

client: I think the story is something like... if they don't like me, it means I'm not good enough for my partner, and eventually they'll start to see that too and pull away from me. It's like their friends are this test I have to pass, and if I fail it, the whole relationship is at risk. I know that probably sounds dramatic, but it feels very real when I'm lying there at 3am.
therapist: It doesn't sound dramatic at all — it sounds like a really painful belief that's been quietly running in the background, linking one social moment to your entire worth as a partner. That's a heavy thing to carry, and it makes so much sense that it feels urgent at 3am when there's nothing to distract from it. I'm curious — is there any evidence from your relationship so far that might challenge the idea that your partner sees you as "not enough"?

client: I mean, yeah, my partner has been really supportive and they tell me they love me pretty regularly, and they were actually excited to introduce me to their friends, which I guess is a good sign. But when I'm in that anxious headspace, it's like my brain just dismisses all of that and goes straight to the worst case anyway. It's frustrating because I can logically see the evidence you're pointing to, but it doesn't seem to make the feeling go away.
therapist: What you're describing is actually one of the most common and frustrating things about anxiety — the logical brain and the emotional brain can feel like they're speaking completely different languages, and knowing something intellectually doesn't automatically make the feeling dissolve. The fact that you *can* see that evidence, even if it doesn't stick yet, is actually really important — it means we have something real to work with. I wonder, when your brain dismisses those positive signs at 3am, what do you think it would take for a piece of evidence to actually *feel* convincing to you, not just make sense on paper?

client: Honestly, I'm not sure anything would feel convincing enough in that moment, because it's like the anxiety has already decided the outcome and it's just looking for proof. Maybe if I actually got through the weekend and they were fine with me, that would help, but then I worry I'll just move the goalposts and find something new to be anxious about. It kind of feels like a losing game sometimes.
therapist: You've just named something really insightful — that the anxiety isn't really *about* the friends, it's more like a pattern that's been finding new targets to latch onto, which is why "passing the test" never quite feels like enough. That awareness is genuinely significant, because it shifts the question from "how do I get these people to like me" to "how do I relate differently to this anxious pattern itself." What do you think has kept this pattern going in your life — is this feeling of needing to prove you're enough something that shows up in other areas too?

client: Yeah, it definitely shows up in other places too, like at work I'm constantly second-guessing whether my contributions are valued, and even with friends I've had for years I sometimes wonder if they actually want me around or just tolerate me. I think part of what keeps it going is that I never really feel like I've earned my place anywhere, so I'm always waiting for people to figure out I'm not worth it. It's kind of exhausting to say out loud, actually, because I don't usually let myself think about how much space this takes up in my life.
therapist: There's something really meaningful about what just happened — you let yourself see the full weight of this, maybe for the first time in a while, and that takes a kind of quiet bravery. What you're describing sounds like a core belief that's been whispering "you haven't earned your place" across so many parts of your life, and that kind of belief is exhausting precisely because it never lets you rest in the good things you already have. I want to gently ask — where do you think that belief first came from, because beliefs this persistent usually have a history?

client: I think it probably goes back to growing up in a household where approval felt really conditional, like I always had to be performing or achieving something to feel like I was okay in my parents' eyes. I don't really like blaming my childhood for things because it feels like making excuses, and my parents weren't terrible people or anything. But I guess if I'm being honest, I never really felt like I was just... enough as I was, without having to prove it.
therapist: What you just shared took real honesty, and I want to gently push back on the idea that recognizing this is "making excuses" — understanding where a belief came from isn't about blame, it's about making sense of something that was taught to you before you had any choice in the matter. A child who only feels okay when they're performing learns, very reasonably, that love is something you earn rather than something you simply have — and that child grew into you, still working so hard to earn a place that was always already yours. I'm wondering, when you imagine a younger version of yourself in that household, what do you wish someone had told them?

client: I think I would have wanted someone to tell that kid that they didn't have to keep trying so hard, that they were already worth being around just as they were. But even as I say that, there's this part of me that kind of rejects it, like it feels nice in theory but I don't know if I actually believe it applies to me. It's strange because I can feel something when I think about that younger version of myself, almost like sadness for them, but it's harder to extend that same compassion to who I am now.
therapist: There's something quietly profound in what you just noticed — you can offer that little kid genuine compassion, but somewhere between then and now, you stopped being someone who deserved it in your own eyes. That gap *is* the work, and the fact that you can feel that sadness for younger you is actually a doorway, because that compassion already exists inside you — it just hasn't learned yet that it's allowed to move forward in time to reach you now. What do you think makes it feel safer or more acceptable to extend kindness to that younger version of yourself than to who you are today?

client: I think it feels safer with the younger version because they were clearly just a kid who didn't know any better, so there's no judgment there. But with who I am now, I feel like I should know better by this point, like I'm an adult and I've had enough time to figure myself out, so if I'm still struggling it must be some kind of failure on my part. It's like compassion for current me feels like letting myself off the hook for something I should have fixed by now.
therapist: There's a really painful double standard hidden in what you just described — the child gets understanding because they "didn't know better," but the adult gets judgment for the same struggle, as if growing up was supposed to have come with a manual that fixed all of this. But I'd gently offer this: the fact that you're still struggling isn't evidence that you've failed to figure yourself out — it's evidence that you're carrying something genuinely heavy that was never yours to carry in the first place, and unlearning a core belief takes time, not willpower. What would it mean for you, even just as an experiment, to consider that needing compassion *now* isn't letting yourself off the hook — but actually the very thing that might finally help you heal?

client: I hear what you're saying and part of me really wants to grab onto it, but there's another part that's worried that if I start being more compassionate with myself I'll just become complacent and stop trying to be better. Like, the self-criticism almost feels functional, as if it's the thing keeping me in check and pushing me to not mess up this weekend or at work or anywhere else. I guess I'm not fully convinced that letting go of that pressure wouldn't just make everything fall apart.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense, and it's actually one of the most common reasons people hold onto self-criticism — it feels like the engine keeping everything running, so letting go feels terrifying rather than relieving. But it's worth gently questioning whether the self-criticism is actually *creating* your success, or whether you're succeeding *despite* it, while also paying the enormous cost of exhaustion, anxiety, and never feeling like enough. What if the part of you that prepares carefully for this weekend, that cares about doing well at work, that shows up for the people you love — what if that part is driven by your values and not by the fear?

client: That's actually a reframe I haven't considered before, and it's making me pause a little because I think I've just always assumed the self-criticism and the caring were the same thing. But I'm not sure I know how to separate them, like practically speaking, how do I stay motivated and prepared for this weekend without the critical voice being part of that process. It feels like trying to take the engine out of a car while it's still moving.
therapist: That's a really honest and important question, and the car analogy is perfect — it makes sense that separating them feels risky when they've been fused together for so long. A gentle place to start might be noticing the *tone* of what's driving you: the critical voice tends to say "you'd better not mess this up or you'll prove you're worthless," while values-based motivation sounds more like "I want to show up well because this relationship matters to me" — same preparation, very different felt experience. As you think about this weekend, which of those two voices do you think you'd actually *want* guiding you into that room?
